old: Its oldest traceable root may have simply meant the living stuff that makes bread rise and drinks ferment.
One old English scholar noted the word appeared 'rare, except in poetry' before it became an everyday drink.
Dutch and German speakers use a word — 'bier' and 'Bier' — that's nearly identical to this one.
clues: This alcoholic drink has a disputed origin: one account traces its name to an ancient Germanic root meaning brewer's yeast, while others link it to a Latin verb meaning to drink.
Brewed from malted grain and hops, it is poured by the pint in pubs, and it is the broad term covering both ale and lager rather than a type of either.
Germans order a Bier and Icelanders a bjór; in English it fills steins at Oktoberfest, comes on tap or in bottles, and lends its name to a pot belly.
